common_name: Pallida Chinese Witch Hazel (Pale Sulfur-Yellow Fragrant Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container or balled stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Pallida' is one of the oldest and most celebrated witch hazel selections, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its pale yellow flowers and exceptional fragrance.

directions: Pallida is a long-established selection of Chinese witch hazel, chosen for softer, pale sulfur-yellow strap-petaled flowers set closer together on the stem than the species, giving a fuller, more luminous winter display against bare branches. Its fragrance is often ranked among the most intensely sweet of any witch hazel, carrying well beyond the plant on a still winter day. Grow it in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, sheltered from harsh winter wind, and expect a broadly vase-shaped, multi-stemmed large shrub with good clear-yellow fall foliage color. It is slow to establish but very long-lived, and needs only minimal pruning to remove crossing or damaged wood after flowering.

common_name: Amethyst Vernal Witch Hazel (Purple-Flowered Ozark Native Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Amethyst' is the only widely available vernal witch hazel selection with true purple-toned flowers rather than the species' typical yellow to red range.

directions: Amethyst is a distinctive selection of the native Ozark witch hazel, notable for strap-petaled flowers in an unusual smoky purple-red tone rather than the yellow, orange, or brick-red typical of the species, opening on bare stems in late winter and closing back up on the coldest nights before reopening as temperatures moderate. Like other vernal witch hazels it carries a spicy, sweet fragrance and blooms earlier in the season than the Asian witch hazel hybrids, giving color and scent in the shade or woodland-edge garden while little else is active. Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, and expect a rounded, multi-stemmed shrub with good gold to orange fall foliage. It tolerates the periodic wet conditions and rocky, gravelly soils of its native Ozark streambank habitat and needs only minimal corrective pruning after flowering.

common_name: Dorothy Wyckoff Pieris (Dark Red Bud Compact Evergreen Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Dorothy Wyckoff is a compact, older cultivar valued for deep maroon-red winter flower buds and purplish-bronze winter foliage.

directions: Dorothy Wyckoff is an older, compact Pieris selection prized for two distinct winter effects: deep maroon-red, unopened flower buds that persist through the cold months before opening to soft pink-blushed white in early spring, and evergreen foliage that takes on a purplish-bronze cast in cold weather before greening up again. Its slower, denser growth habit fits a foundation planting or shaded border better than larger-growing Pieris cultivars. Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying winter wind, and mulch to conserve soil moisture and acidity. Prune lightly right after flowering only if needed, since Pieris sets next year's buds soon after bloom finishes.

common_name: Cavatine Pieris (True Dwarf Heavy-Blooming Evergreen Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Cavatine is a true dwarf, low-mounding selection well suited to small foundation beds where larger Pieris cultivars would quickly outgrow the space.

directions: Cavatine is a true dwarf Pieris, forming a dense, low, spreading mound far smaller than the species, yet flowering just as heavily, with upright to slightly arching clusters of small white, urn-shaped, lightly fragrant flowers in early to mid spring. Its compact scale makes it a practical choice for small foundation beds, rock gardens, and mixed shrub borders where the typical 8- to 10-foot Pieris species would eventually overwhelm the space. Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and winter wind, mulching to hold moisture and soil acidity. It is slow-growing and needs very little pruning to keep its naturally tidy, mounded form.

common_name: Little Heath Pieris (Variegated Dwarf Pink-Tinged Evergreen Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Little Heath is a slow, dwarf, white-margined variegated selection grown chiefly for year-round foliage interest rather than heavy bloom.

directions: Little Heath is a slow-growing dwarf Pieris grown primarily for its foliage, with narrow, glossy leaves edged in a crisp creamy-white margin that takes on a soft pink flush on new growth in spring and again in cold weather, giving it interest across every season rather than relying on its light, sparse clusters of white spring flowers. Its diminutive, dense, mounding habit makes it useful for small-space foundation plantings, container culture, and the front of a shaded mixed border where a larger Pieris would be out of scale. Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying winter wind, and mulch to help hold consistent soil moisture and acidity. It requires very little pruning beyond removing any stems that revert to solid green.

common_name: Curly Red Leucothoe (Wavy-Leaf Red New-Growth Coast Doghobble)

planting.note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, highly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Curly Red is a selection of native Coastal Doghobble with distinctively wavy, twisted leaf margins and bright red-bronze new growth.

directions: Curly Red is a selection of native Coastal Doghobble bred for distinctively wavy, twisted leaf margins that add fine textural interest beyond the arching, cascading habit typical of the species. New foliage emerges a bright wine-red to bronze and holds color well before settling into glossy dark green, with a repeat flush of color again in cool fall and winter weather. Small white, urn-shaped flowers appear along the undersides of the arching stems in spring, though the plant is grown mainly for its foliage. Like the species, it is exceptionally shade-tolerant and thrives in moist, highly acidic soil under dense tree canopy where few other broadleaf evergreens perform well, making it a strong groundcover or low border shrub for a shaded, woodland-edge planting.
